claim: Synchronous neuronal ensembles play a pivotal role in the consolidation of long-term memory in the hippocampus.
source: Synchronous neuronal ensembles play a pivotal role in the consolidation of long-term memory in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established understanding in the field.

claim: Synchronous ensembles comprising approximately 40% of CA1 pyramidal neurons fire simultaneously in brief windows (~25ms) during immobility and locomotion in novel exploration.
source: We found synchronous ensembles comprising approximately 40% of CA1 pyramidal neurons, firing simultaneously in brief windows (~25ms) during immobility and locomotion in novel exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage imaging experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Synchronous ensembles were not associated with contralateral ripple oscillations.
source: Notably, these synchronous ensembles were not associated with contralateral ripple oscillations but were instead phase-locked to theta waves recorded in the contralateral CA1 region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between synchronous ensembles and LFP recordings.

claim: Synchronous ensembles were phase-locked to theta waves recorded in the contralateral CA1 region.
source: Notably, these synchronous ensembles were not associated with contralateral ripple oscillations but were instead phase-locked to theta waves recorded in the contralateral CA1 region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing theta modulation of synchronous ensembles.

claim: The subthreshold membrane potentials of neurons exhibited coherent intracellular theta oscillations with a depolarizing peak at the moment of synchrony.
source: Moreover, the subthreshold membrane potentials of neurons exhibited coherent intracellular theta oscillations with a depolarizing peak at the moment of synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by voltage imaging data showing subthreshold membrane voltage dynamics.

claim: Among newly formed place cells, pairs with more robust synchronization during locomotion displayed more distinct place-specific activities.
source: Among newly formed place cells, pairs with more robust synchronization during locomotion displayed more distinct place-specific activities.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of spatial tuning and synchronization strength correlations.

claim: Synchronous ensembles play a role in coordinating place cells of different place fields.
source: These findings underscore the role of synchronous ensembles in coordinating place cells of different place fields.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings regarding synchronization and place field relationships.

claim: The hippocampus is a crucial region for long-term memory formation.
source: The hippocampus, a crucial region for long-term memory formation (Harris et al., 2003; Squire and Wixted, 2011), has been a focal point of synchronous ensemble studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synchronous ensembles among CA1 pyramidal cells are predominantly observed during sharp-wave ripples.
source: In the hippocampus, synchronous ensembles among CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) are predominantly observed during sharp-wave ripples, the brain waves associated with memory consolidation (Buzsáki, 2015; Nádasdy et al., 1999; Cheng and Frank, 2008; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Liu et al., 2023; Colgin, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During sharp-wave ripples, 10–18% of CA1PCs generate spikes, particularly during offline consummatory behavioral states or sleep.
source: During these events, 10–18% of CA1PCs generate spikes, particularly during offline consummatory behavioral states or sleep (Buzsáki and da Silva, 2012; Csicsvari et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synchronous ensembles firing action potentials in short windows of 10–30 ms enhance information processing.
source: Furthermore, synchronous ensembles firing action potentials in short windows of 10–30 ms enhance information processing (Harris et al., 2003) and discriminate distinct behavioral contingencies (El-Gaby et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have identified correlated activities among place cells during theta oscillation, where 1–3% of place cells' spikes co-activate in a forward order matching animals' trajectory in the theta cycles.
source: Previous studies have identified correlated activities among place cells during theta oscillation, where 1–3% of place cells' spikes co-activate in a forward order matching animals' trajectory in the theta cycles when animals' locations overlap in the place fields of these cells (Skaggs, 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Population synchrony on shorter timescales (10–30ms) is speculated to be reduced by the presence of theta oscillations.
source: Population synchrony on shorter timescales (10–30ms) is speculated to be reduced by the presence of theta oscillations (Mizuseki and Buzsaki, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The subthreshold membrane voltage (subVm), influenced by synaptic inputs and intrinsic conductances, directly triggers spiking activity.
source: The subthreshold membrane voltage (subVm), influenced by synaptic inputs and intrinsic conductances, directly triggers spiking activity (Lee and Brecht, 2018; Petersen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Properties of subVm support the organization of neuronal representation.
source: Additionally, properties of subVm support the organization of neuronal representation (Giocomo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Correlated membrane potentials have been proposed to underlie the synchrony of neuronal ensembles.
source: Although correlated membrane potentials have been proposed to underlie the synchrony of neuronal ensembles (Lampl et al., 1999; Poulet and Petersen, 2008), multicellular recordings of subVms have not yet provided direct experimental evidence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mice moved at a speed of 8.3±0.9 cm/s during locomotion in novel exploration.
source: In novel exploration, mice moved at a speed of 8.3±0.9 cm/s during locomotion (speed >3 cm/s) and spent 53 ± 7% and 36 ± 6% of their time in locomotion and immobility (speed <1 cm/s), respectively (n=5 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tracking.

claim: Mice spent 53 ± 7% of their time in locomotion during novel exploration.
source: In novel exploration, mice moved at a speed of 8.3±0.9 cm/s during locomotion (speed >3 cm/s) and spent 53 ± 7% and 36 ± 6% of their time in locomotion and immobility (speed <1 cm/s), respectively (n=5 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tracking.

claim: Mice spent 36 ± 6% of their time in immobility during novel exploration.
source: In novel exploration, mice moved at a speed of 8.3±0.9 cm/s during locomotion (speed >3 cm/s) and spent 53 ± 7% and 36 ± 6% of their time in locomotion and immobility (speed <1 cm/s), respectively (n=5 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tracking.

claim: Mice completed 10±2.5 laps during the 180 s imaging periods in novel exploration.
source: Meanwhile, they completed 10±2.5 laps during the 180 s imaging periods (n=5 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tracking.

claim: 14±4 cells were imaged per field of view, and in total, 71 cells were imaged from 5 fields of view in 5 mice.
source: For voltage imaging, we expressed the voltage indicator Voltron2 (Abdelfattah et al., 2023) in CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) that were born on embryonic day (E) 14.5, allowing us to measure both suprathreshold and subthreshold membrane potentials from multiple CA1PCs (14±4 cells imaged per field of view (mean ±s.d.) and, in total, 71 cells imaged from 5 fields of view in 5 mice; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage imaging.

claim: Neurons labeled on E14.5 located more on the deep side of the pyramidal layer than those labeled on E17.5.
source: Consistent with previous studies, neurons labeled on E14.5 located more on the deep side of the pyramidal layer than those labeled on E17.5 (t(601)=22.8, p<0.0001, Student's t-test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D; Angevine Jr, 1965; Bayer, 1980; Cavalieri et al., 2021; Cembrowski et al., 2016; Huszár et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: The mean firing rates of cells ranged from 2.3 to 4.3 Hz (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 3.2 Hz.
source: The mean firing rates of cells ranged from 2.3 to 4.3 Hz (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 3.2 Hz (n=71 cells, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from voltage imaging.

claim: Most CA1PCs exhibited elevated mean firing rates during immobility relative to locomotion.
source: Additionally, most CA1PCs exhibited elevated mean firing rates during immobility relative to locomotion, and their firing rates showed a negative correlation with the animals' speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C), consistent with previous research (Adam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research.

claim: CA1PC firing rates showed a negative correlation with the animals' speed.
source: Additionally, most CA1PCs exhibited elevated mean firing rates during immobility relative to locomotion, and their firing rates showed a negative correlation with the animals' speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C), consistent with previous research (Adam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous research.

claim: The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the peak in the grand average CCG measured 23±14ms.
source: The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the peak in the grand average CCG measured 23±14ms (mean ±s.d., n=71 cells from 5 sessions; Figure 1F), indicating the timescale of the population synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: 63% of cell pairs showed significant peaks in pairwise CCGs compared to jittered data.
source: Furthermore, pairwise CCGs of many cell pairs showed significant peaks compared to jittered data (percentage of significant pairs: 63% (median), n=497 pairs, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: Among pairs with significant peaks, the absolute values of the peak lags ranged from 0.8 to 4.3ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 2.1ms.
source: Among pairs with significant peaks, the absolute values of the peak lags ranged from 0.8 to 4.3ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 2.1ms, and the FWHM of the peaks ranged from 20 to 46ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 30ms (n=315 pairs, Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: The FWHM of CCG peaks ranged from 20 to 46ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 30ms for pairs with significant peaks.
source: Among pairs with significant peaks, the absolute values of the peak lags ranged from 0.8 to 4.3ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 2.1ms, and the FWHM of the peaks ranged from 20 to 46ms (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 30ms (n=315 pairs, Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: There was over a 7.8-fold increase in synchronous events in the original data compared to jittered controls.
source: Using the same criterion for event detection, we observed over a 7.8-fold increase in synchronous events in the original data compared to jittered controls (mean event rate: 0.94±0.17 Hz for the original data, 0.12±0.01 Hz for the jittered data, n=10 segments, p=0.002, W=55, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing original and jittered spike trains.

claim: The ensemble sizes ranged from 32% to 53% (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 42%.
source: The ensemble sizes ranged from 32% to 53% (25th-75th percentiles) with a median of 42%, which were larger than the synchronous ensemble sizes associated with ripples (Buzsáki and da Silva, 2012; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to previous research.

claim: The FWHMs of grand average CCGs were broader in the immobility group compared to the locomotion group.
source: Nevertheless, the FWHMs of grand average CCGs were broader in the immobility group compared to the locomotion group (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing immobility and locomotion conditions.

claim: Synchronous events occurred more frequently during immobility compared to locomotion.
source: Synchronous events occurred more frequently during immobility compared to locomotion (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing immobility and locomotion conditions.

claim: Ensemble sizes were significantly larger in the immobility group compared to the locomotion group.
source: Additionally, ensemble sizes were significantly larger in the immobility group compared to the locomotion group (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing immobility and locomotion conditions.

claim: C-ripples were detected in three of the five recording sessions, and all occurred during immobility.
source: C-ripples were detected in three of the five recording sessions, and all occurred during immobility (mean c-ripple rate: 0.04±0.02 Hz during immobility, 0 Hz during locomotion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LFP recordings.

claim: There was no co-occurrence of c-ripples and synchronous ensembles.
source: Remarkably, there was no co-occurrence of c-ripples and synchronous ensembles (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing the temporal relationship between c-ripples and synchronous ensembles.

claim: 85% of cells displayed c-ripple modulation indexes of –1, indicating complete suppression of their spiking activities during c-ripples.
source: Indexes of most cells were negative, and a striking 85% of cells displayed c-ripple modulation indexes of –1, indicating complete suppression of their spiking activities during c-ripples (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing c-ripple modulation of spiking.

claim: Approximately 40% of the recorded neurons participated in synchronous ensembles in immobilized mice.
source: Approximately 40% of the recorded neurons participated in synchronous ensembles, indicating robust synchronous activity involving a substantial proportion of the recorded cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immobilized mice.

claim: 1052 synchronous ensembles and 174 c-ripple episodes were detected across imaging sessions in immobilized mice.
source: In total, 1052 synchronous ensembles and 174 c-ripple episodes were detected across these imaging sessions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immobilized mice.

claim: 90% of neurons showed significant negative spiking modulation during c-ripples in immobilized mice.
source: At the single-cell level, 90% of neurons showed significant negative spiking modulation during c-ripples, with c-ripple modulation indexes close to –1, indicating strong suppression of spiking (Figure 4Ai).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immobilized mice.

claim: Nearly all cells exhibited decreased fluorescence during c-ripples compared to baseline in immobilized mice.
source: This suppression extended to subthreshold membrane potentials, as nearly all cells exhibited decreased fluorescence during c-ripples compared to baseline (Figure 4Bi and Ci).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immobilized mice.

claim: Mean firing rates were significantly reduced in the familiar group compared to the novel group.
source: Mean firing rates were significantly reduced in the familiar group compared to the novel group (Familiar group: 1.1–5.2 Hz (25th-75th percentiles), median = 2.3 Hz, n=66 cells, 6 sessions, 4 mice; Novel group: 1.7–6.0 Hz (25th-75th percentiles), median = 4.2 Hz, n=111 cells, 6 sessions, 6 mice, p=0.0083, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing novel and familiar contexts.

claim: 15% of the neurons in the familiar group exhibited significantly positive spiking modulation by c-ripples.
source: Additionally, 15% of the neurons in the familiar group exhibited significantly positive spiking modulation by c-ripples, while fewer cells showed negative modulation compared to the novel group (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing novel and familiar contexts.

claim: Synchronous event frequencies were significantly lower in the familiar context.
source: Finally, synchronous event frequencies were significantly lower in the familiar context, indicating weaker synchronous activities under familiar conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing novel and familiar contexts.

claim: Synchronous ensembles displayed a high level of modulation by LFP theta oscillation (modulation strength: 0.61±0.05 during immobility and 0.74±0.04 during locomotion).
source: In line with the previous result, synchronous ensembles displayed a high level of modulation by LFP theta oscillation (modulation strength: 0.61±0.05 during immobility and 0.74±0.04 during locomotion, n=5 sessions).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing theta modulation of synchronous ensembles.

claim: Spikes participating in both immobility and locomotion synchrony were strongly coupled to the subVm theta oscillation of neurons.
source: Spikes participating in both immobility and locomotion synchrony were strongly coupled to the subVm theta oscillation of neurons, with the mean preferred phase being in the latter half of the rising phase closer to subVm theta peaks (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing subVm theta modulation of spikes.

claim: Spikes not participating in synchronous ensembles had weaker modulation strength compared to spikes involved in synchrony.
source: Conversely, spikes not participating in synchronous ensembles had weaker modulation strength compared to spikes involved in synchrony (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing spikes participating and not participating in synchronous ensembles.

claim: The subVm theta coherences were increased in both immobility and locomotion groups (immobility: 0.50, locomotion: 0.40, median).
source: Furthermore, the subVm theta coherences were increased in both groups (immobility: 0.50, locomotion: 0.40, median, n=511 pairs) and were negatively correlated with soma distances (immobility: –0.46, locomotion: –0.48, n=511 pairs, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing subVm coherence.

claim: SubVm theta coherences were negatively correlated with soma distances (immobility: –0.46, locomotion: –0.48).
source: Furthermore, the subVm theta coherences were increased in both groups (immobility: 0.50, locomotion: 0.40, median, n=511 pairs) and were negatively correlated with soma distances (immobility: –0.46, locomotion: –0.48, n=511 pairs, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing subVm coherence and soma distances.

claim: Spiking at specific theta cycles plays a major role in driving population synchrony.
source: The finding indicates spiking at specific theta cycles plays a major role in driving population synchrony.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of theta cycle randomization.

claim: On average, 40% of cells displayed selective spatial tunings of their spiking activities and were qualified as place cells.
source: On average, 40% of cells displayed selective spatial tunings of their spiking activities and were qualified as place cells (Go et al., 2021; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing spatial tuning.

claim: Cell pairs with more precisely co-active spikes during locomotion exhibited more distinct place-tuning profiles.
source: In other words, cell pairs with more precisely co-active spikes during locomotion exhibited more distinct place-tuning profiles (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing the relationship between synchronization and spatial tuning.

claim: Synchronization strength during immobility showed little correlation with the similarity of spatial tunings among place cell pairs.
source: On the other hand, synchronization strength during immobility showed little correlation with the similarity of spatial tunings among place cell pairs, suggesting that correlated activities at the millisecond timescale do not extend to slow, behavioral-relevant timescales (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analyzing the relationship between synchronization and spatial tuning during immobility.

claim: Theta oscillations are typically associated with the sequential activation of neurons over time, resulting in reduced neuronal synchrony.
source: Theta oscillations are typically associated with the sequential activation of neurons over time, resulting in reduced neuronal synchrony (Mizuseki and Buzsaki, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Type 1 theta, or translational theta, occurs during voluntary movements and is sensitive to N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) blockers.
source: For example, type 1 theta, or translational theta, occurs during voluntary movements and is sensitive to N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) blockers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about theta oscillation types.

claim: Type 2 theta, or attentional theta, is slightly slower and is blocked by muscarinic receptor antagonists, emerging during states of arousal or attention.
source: On the other hand, type 2 theta, or attentional theta, is slightly slower and is blocked by muscarinic receptor antagonists, emerging during states of arousal or attention, such as when entering a new environment (Sainsbury et al., 1987; Sainsbury, 1998; Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about theta oscillation types supported by citations.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the medial septum excite downstream CA1PCs during theta oscillations, leading to increased firing rates and membrane potentials.
source: During theta oscillations, cholinergic neurons in the medial septum excite downstream CA1PCs, leading to increased firing rates and membrane potentials (Nakajima et al., 1986; Markram and Segal, 1990; Fraser and MacVicar, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Theta power correlates positively with learning performance.
source: Specifically, theta power correlates positively with learning performance (Landfield et al., 1972; Berry and Thompson, 1978; Belchior et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perturbing generation of theta waves leads to impairment in memory acquisition.
source: Perturbing generation of theta waves leads to impairment in memory acquisition (Winson, 1978; Mitchell et al., 1982; Mizumori et al., 1990; M'Harzi and Jarrard, 1992; Wang et al., 2015), while electrical stimulation restoring theta rhythms rescues learning performance (McNaughton et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased spike-theta coherence correlates with better memory.
source: Furthermore, increased spike-theta coherence correlates with better memory, and stimulations that boost theta phase-locking of spikes enhance memory (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Rutishauser et al., 2010; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CA1PCs are known to exhibit weaker recurrent connectivity than that of CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Although CA1PCs are known to exhibit weaker recurrent connectivity than that of CA3 pyramidal neurons, CA1PCs did communicate through monosynaptic connections (Deuchars and Thomson, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CA1PC connections can be dynamically adjusted by the spike-timing-dependent plasticity mechanism.
source: These connections can be dynamically adjusted by the spike-timing-dependent plasticity mechanism (Caporale and Dan, 2008; Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998), and therefore could be affected by the transient population synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Multiple pyramidal neurons converge onto a single interneuron, and individual connections are often weak and unreliable.
source: Multiple pyramidal neurons converge onto a single interneuron, and individual connections are often weak and unreliable (English et al., 2017; Ali et al., 1998; Ali et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: This connectivity scheme requires multiple pyramidal neurons spiking synchronously within the time window of synaptic integration to effectively activate postsynaptic neurons.
source: This connectivity scheme requires multiple pyramidal neurons spiking synchronously within the time window of synaptic integration to effectively activate postsynaptic neurons (English et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Prior studies in sensory systems have commonly revealed that neurons with synchronous activities typically share similar sensory responses.
source: Prior studies in sensory systems have commonly revealed that neurons with synchronous activities typically share similar sensory responses (Alonso et al., 1996; Engel et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
